raw_text:
Bioresorbable vascular scaffolds (BVS) were conceived to solve a paradox of contemporary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI): metallic drug-eluting stents (DES) are highly effective, yet they permanently cage the vessel, may impair vasomotion, complicate future bypass or imaging, and can remain a substrate for very-late failure. Early feasibility studies of the poly-L-lactic acid everolimus-eluting Absorb scaffold showed acceptable acute success, serial multimodality imaging, late lumen preservation, and evidence of vasomotor recovery after resorption [1], [2]. Iterative redesign improved radial support and reduced early scaffold shrinkage in ABSORB Cohort B [3], with 2- and 5-year imaging suggesting late lumen enlargement and disappearance of strut footprints in selected simple lesions [4], [5].

The randomized ABSORB II program formalized the hypothesis that “vascular restoration” might translate into clinical and functional benefit [6]. At 1 year, Absorb achieved broadly similar clinical outcomes to Xience but with less acute gain and more residual stenosis [7]. At 3 years, however, the trial did not demonstrate superior vasomotion or late lumen advantage and showed higher target-vessel myocardial infarction and scaffold thrombosis, especially during the bioresorption phase [8]. Larger pivotal studies reinforced this pattern. ABSORB III met noninferiority for target-lesion failure at 1 year in relatively noncomplex lesions [9], but 3-year follow-up showed increased target-lesion failure and device thrombosis, particularly in small vessels [10]. ABSORB IV, which mandated better lesion selection and implantation technique, improved early outcomes but did not eliminate the late penalty: at 5 years, target-lesion failure remained higher with BVS, while event curves appeared similar after approximately 3 years, consistent with completion of resorption [11], [12].

Regional randomized trials added important external validity. ABSORB Japan and ABSORB China generally showed similar early angiographic and clinical outcomes in selected lesions, but their careful vessel sizing and lower small-vessel enrollment limited generalizability [13], [14]. Registry data such as ABSORB EXTEND demonstrated feasibility in broader practice but also highlighted the importance of lesion complexity, operator learning, and post-dilatation [15]. In ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction, the TROFI II trial showed noninferior optical healing at 6 months, yet STEMI use remained biologically attractive rather than definitively proven safer [16]. In routine all-comers PCI, the AIDA trial was decisive: target-vessel failure was not significantly different, but scaffold thrombosis was substantially higher with Absorb, prompting clinical retrenchment [17].

Mechanistically, first-generation polymeric BVS failed for convergent reasons. Thick struts impaired deliverability and disturbed flow; limited expansion capacity increased underexpansion risk; polymer dismantling during resorption could create malapposition, discontinuity, and thrombogenic intraluminal material; and implantation in small or calcified vessels magnified these hazards [18]. Pooled analyses confirmed that meticulous “PSP” technique—prepare the lesion, size appropriately, and post-dilate—reduced but did not abolish risk [19]. Expert consensus therefore emphasized avoidance of small vessels, aggressive lesion preparation, high-pressure noncompliant post-dilatation within expansion limits, intravascular imaging when feasible, and prolonged antiplatelet vigilance [20]. Meta-analyses consistently found higher myocardial infarction and definite/probable scaffold thrombosis with Absorb compared with contemporary everolimus-eluting metallic stents at mid-term follow-up [21], [22], [23]. The final ABSORB pooled analysis suggests the excess risk is concentrated before 3 years, with fewer very-late events after bioresorption, but no clear net clinical superiority has emerged [24].

The field has therefore shifted from validating the concept to redesigning the platform. Magnesium-based resorbable metallic scaffolds offer more stent-like mechanical behavior, faster resorption, smoother electropolished struts, and potentially lower thrombogenicity. The PROGRESS-AMS bare magnesium scaffold proved feasibility but suffered excessive late loss from rapid loss of radial strength [25]. Drug-eluting magnesium iterations improved performance: BIOSOLVE-I with paclitaxel-eluting DREAMS demonstrated acceptable 12-month safety [26], and BIOSOLVE-II with sirolimus-eluting DREAMS 2G/Magmaris showed low target-lesion failure and no definite/probable scaffold thrombosis in selected lesions [27]. Imaging studies documented progressive strut integration and resorption [28]. Nonetheless, randomized MAGSTEMI data in STEMI did not prove superior vasomotion and raised concerns about angiographic efficacy and target-lesion failure versus metallic sirolimus-eluting stents [29]; 3-year results remained hypothesis-generating [30].

In current PCI, bioresorbable scaffolds should not be viewed as routine substitutes for ultrathin contemporary DES. Their legacy is instructive: transient scaffolding is biologically appealing, but clinical benefit requires DES-like acute gain, very low thrombogenicity throughout degradation, broad deliverability, and forgiving implantation characteristics. Future success will likely depend on thinner struts, stronger yet faster-resorbing materials, imaging-guided trials, and targeting niches where absence of permanent metal is most valuable—young patients, long lesions requiring future surgical options, or lesions where vascular function matters. Until such evidence exists, BVS remain an important technological chapter rather than a default PCI strategy.
